name: Hairy chest transplant / body hair transplant

image.caption: Hairy chest transplant / body hair transplant

lead: Some men consider moving follicles to the chest to get visibly fuller chest hair. Body hair transplant uses follicular unit extraction (FUE) to move individual follicles from one area to another; looksmaxxing posts about a hairy chest transplant apply it to the chest itself.

Follicular units of one to four hairs are extracted with small punches and implanted individually, and transplanted hair is described as keeping the growth characteristics of its donor area. Published case series and small studies mostly cover body hair as donor supply for the scalp, and uses in scars and vitiligo, including a 122-patient series. No studies of transplanting hair onto the chest for appearance were found.

paras: A surgeon harvests follicles from the beard, chest or limbs and places them in the target area in a single procedure. Body hair has a high share of follicles in the resting phase, which one study addressed by shaving donor sites days before extraction.

Reported issues include temporary shedding of transplanted hair, variable graft survival and the general risks of surgery. Reference sources say body hair differs from scalp hair in texture and growth rate. Cost varies widely by country.

angle.text: FUE moves follicles from the beard or body to the chest so the grafts add hair where it is sparse. Published work mostly covers body hair as donor supply for the scalp, and cosmetic chest transplants have barely been studied.

lead: Body hair transplantation (BHT) is a form of follicular unit extraction (FUE) in which follicles are moved between body regions. It is used in two directions: taking hair from the beard, chest or limbs to add density elsewhere, most often the scalp,[1][2] and, in what looksmaxxing discussions call a hairy chest transplant, placing hair onto a sparse chest.[3] Either way, the aim in appearance terms is to add hair where it is wanted. Wikipedia's overview of hair transplantation lists chest hair among the sites that transplantation can be used to restore, alongside beard, eyebrows, eyelashes and scars.[4]

Hair that grows on the chest is androgen-dependent: chest and abdominal skin carry fine vellus hair from childhood, and in late puberty and adulthood men grow increasing amounts of terminal hair there, with the amount set by hormone levels and by the sensitivity of the follicles, which varies by body area and by genetics.[5] Men whose chest stays sparse therefore sometimes consider moving follicles there, and some clinics advertise chest transplants using hair from the back of the scalp.[3]

The published literature is mostly about the opposite direction. Body hair is used as additional donor supply for balding scalps and for scars, cicatricial alopecia and vitiligo.[1][6][7][8] A 2017 review describes BHT as useful alone or combined with scalp hair in advanced baldness, for improving hairlines, and in scarring alopecia where scalp donor hair is scarce.[9] A 122-patient series reported outcomes of body hair transplanted to the scalp,[1] and a 2019 study compared the survival of scalp, beard and chest grafts.[10] Peer-reviewed studies of transplanting hair onto the chest for appearance were not found; the cosmetic chest-recipient procedure is described mainly on clinic pages.
infobox: Beard, chest, trunk, limbs; or back of scalp for chest recipient[9][3]
Chest 75.3% and beard 94.7% at 1 year in a 5-patient study[10]

paras: FUE removes follicular units individually with small punches and places them in recipient sites, avoiding the linear scar of strip harvesting; it is described as time-consuming and technique-dependent [2]. Reference sources say BHT can only be done by FUE and requires an experienced surgeon, and that texture and growth-rate differences between body and scalp hair should be considered [4].
Many body hairs are in the resting (telogen) phase and occur as single-hair units. One group proposed shaving donor body hair four days before extraction to identify anagen hairs [11].

Clinics describe two practical versions. In the first, body follicles from chest, back, arms, legs or beard are moved to the scalp, beard or other thinning areas, mainly when scalp donor supply is limited. In the second, the chest or abdomen is the recipient: one clinic says the procedure adds fullness and density to thin or patchy chest growth, using FUE with donor follicles usually taken from the back of the scalp and placed in patterns meant to mimic natural growth.[3] The same clinic estimates available graft counts of about 1,000 to 5,000 from the chest, 1,000 to 4,000 from the back and 500 to 3,000 from the beard.[3]

Wikipedia describes hair transplantation as moving follicles from a donor site to a recipient site, with grafts placed in natural groupings of one to four hairs to mimic original orientation [4]. Two harvesting methods exist: strip harvesting, which leaves a linear scar, and FUE, which uses small punches (0.6 to 1.0 mm in Wikipedia's account) and leaves tiny punctate marks, with recovery usually under a week; FUE takes longer and costs more [4]. The modern era began in the late 1950s when New York dermatologist Norman Orentreich showed that grafts are 'donor dominant', continuing to grow as they would at their original site, and Walter Unger later defined the 'safe donor zone' [4]. Because transplanted hair keeps the behaviour of its origin, body hair retains body-hair traits of length, thickness and growth cycle [4][9].

sections.h: Body hair as a donor source
paras: The 2017 review notes that FUE leaves no linear scar and so suits harvesting from beard, chest and extremities in hirsute individuals, but that body hair may not match scalp hair in thickness, length or hair cycle, and that harvesting takes more time and skill than regular scalp FUE; it highlights use in advanced baldness (Norwood grade five and above) [9]. In the 122-patient series, surveyed patients (79 responded, at a mean 2.9 years) gave mean scores of at least 7.8 out of 10 for healing, growth and overall satisfaction, comparable to patients whose transplants included scalp donor hair [1]. A 2013 case report described complete repigmentation of a stable vitiligo patch by 12 weeks after body hair transplant [7].

Hair transplantation has a long history: Wikipedia dates successful implantation of scalp hair onto favus scars to Menahem Hodara in 1897, Japanese surgeons used small grafts for eyebrows and lashes in the 1930s, and New York dermatologist Norman Orentreich's work from the late 1950s established modern transplantation for male pattern baldness.[4] Follicular unit techniques were refined in the 1980s and 1990s, and robotic FUE devices received FDA clearance for hair restoration in 2009 (NeoGraft) and 2011 (ARTAS).[4]

Body hair was used as an adjunct once FUE, which leaves no linear scar, made harvesting from beard, chest and limbs feasible.[9] Published reports include a 2008 letter on body hair transplanted into a wide donor scar,[8] a 2010 paper on identifying growing body hairs before extraction,[11] a 2012 case report on cicatricial alopecia,[6] a 2013 vitiligo case report,[7] the 2016 122-patient series covering 2005 to 2011,[1] and a 2019 comparison of scalp, beard and chest hair survival.[10]

sections.h: Body hair biology and transplant behaviour
paras: Transplanted hair is described as donor dominant: Wikipedia says Orentreich showed grafts continue to grow as they would at their original site, which is why body hair keeps body-hair traits of length, thickness and cycle after transplantation.[4] The 2017 review notes that body hair thickness, length and hair cycle may not match scalp hair.[9] One clinic describes chest follicles as often coarser and growing as single strands, with a shorter growth phase so they may not reach scalp length.[3][12]

A 2010 paper from a New Delhi clinic notes that 40 to 70 percent of body hair is in the resting (telogen) phase at any time, and proposes wet-shaving donor areas about four days before extraction so that growing hairs, which have lengthened, can be identified; it reports that wet shaving can cause mild folliculitis.[11][13]

FUE extracts follicular units individually under local anaesthesia, using small punches of about 0.6 to 1.0 mm in Wikipedia's account, then places them into small recipient incisions in a chosen density and angle; recovery is usually less than a week for scalp FUE, though sessions are longer and costlier than strip surgery.[4] Wikipedia says body hair transplant can only be performed by FUE and requires an experienced FUE surgeon.[4]

One clinic gives a recovery timeline for chest work: swelling, redness and crusting in the first week; shedding of the transplanted shafts at weeks two to three, described as normal; sparse appearance and possible temporary shedding of native hair at one to three months; roughly 60 to 70 percent of final density by month six; and full results at nine to twelve months.[3] This is a clinic account rather than a published series.

A series of 122 patients with adequate body hair who received hair from the beard, trunk and extremities on bald scalp areas between 2005 and 2011 was published in 2016. Of the 79 patients who answered a survey at a mean of 2.9 years, mean scores were at least 7.8 out of 10 for healing, growth and overall satisfaction, comparable to patients whose transplants included scalp donor hair.[1] An accompanying commentary also appeared.[14]

A 2019 study from a New Delhi clinic in the Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery transplanted one follicular unit each from scalp, beard and chest into three blocks on the scalps of five men with Norwood grade 6 to 7 baldness, 150 grafts per site. At one year survival was 94.7 percent for beard, 88.7 percent for scalp and 75.3 percent for chest; anagen effluvium at two months was about 30 percent for beard, 40 percent for scalp and over 50 percent for chest. One patient had folliculitis that resolved with topical antibiotics, and four of five had minor donor-site hypopigmentation. The authors concluded that beard and chest hair can be a good donor source and noted the small sample and short follow-up.[10][15]

Other reports cover body hair transplant for cicatricial alopecia,[6] repigmentation of a stable vitiligo patch within 12 weeks in a 28-year-old man,[7] and a wide donor scar.[8] A 2021 review lists body hair transplant among the uses of FUE alongside androgenetic alopecia, alopecia areata, facial hair restoration and vitiligo.[2] A registered vitiligo hair-transplant trial was withdrawn,[16] and a trial of a protocol to improve follicle survival in FUE is registered and not yet recruiting.[17] No studies of transplanting hair onto the chest for cosmetic purposes were found.

Reference sources list temporary shedding (shock loss), reduced graft survival with smoking or alcohol, and infection requiring antibiotics in some cases; some surgeons report lower graft success for FUE than strip surgery.[4] Clinic sources say non-scalp grafts survive at roughly 60 to 80 percent compared with 90 percent or more for scalp-to-scalp grafts.[3] Body hair can differ from scalp hair in texture and growth rate, and one London clinic says chest hair cannot be the only donor source for a completely bald man.[4][12]

Costs per graft are reported to range from about US$1 in Turkey to US$7 in Canada.[4] Wikipedia also reports that FUE is physically demanding and has a learning curve for surgeons, and the 2017 review says body hair harvesting takes more time and skill than regular scalp FUE.[4][9] Candidacy criteria listed by one clinic include adequate donor density, realistic expectations and no active skin infection in donor or recipient areas.[3]

Related approaches include scalp FUE and strip surgery,[4] beard and eyebrow transplants,[4] and shaving, waxing or laser removal at the opposite end of body hair grooming; Wikipedia notes athletes such as swimmers and bodybuilders sometimes remove body hair to show muscle definition.[5]

lore.intro: Chest hair transplants are promoted mainly by clinics and discussed in hair-restoration publications; claims below are attributed to those sources.[3][9]

claims.claim: Chest hair can be used to supplement scalp donor hair for balding men.
Chest transplanted hair survives as well as scalp hair.
A hairy chest can be created by moving scalp follicles to the chest.
Body hair looks identical to scalp hair after transplant.
Shaving donor hair beforehand identifies the best grafts.
Body hair transplant can repigment vitiligo patches.

timeline.event: Menahem Hodara implants scalp hair onto scars left bald by favus.[4]
Norman Orentreich begins grafting for male pattern baldness and shows grafts are donor dominant.[4]
Period of the 122-patient body hair FUE series.[1]
Letter reports body hair transplanted into a wide donor scar.[8]
NeoGraft becomes the first FDA-cleared robotic device for hair restoration.[4]
A preshaving protocol to identify growing body hairs is published.[11]
The ARTAS robotic system is FDA approved for harvesting follicular units.[4]
Case report of body hair transplant repigmenting a vitiligo patch.[7]
The 122-patient series and a commentary are published in Aesthetic Surgery Journal.[1][14]
Review 'Body to Scalp: Evolving Trends in Body Hair Transplantation' is published.[9]
Comparative study of scalp, beard and chest hair survival is published.[10]
